records.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts (execution 149.118) scored 2/8; every one of the six failures reasoned that a speaker who knows their own value plus the public number can just subtract or divide, declared both readings of the public number impossible, and then filled the box with an arbitrary divisor (143 three times, 11 once) or burned the 16k cap looping on that contradiction (three of eight hit finish_reason=length). The revision keeps the incumbent's short elimination frame but names the mechanism the failures skipped: residual uncertainty can live entirely in the unstated coordinate, so candidates must be counted jointly across all coordinates rather than inside one committed reading, and a dead end signals over-credited knowledge rather than a contradictory puzzle.

All 8 rollouts scored 1 so training is saturated; the diagnostic signal is that the two longest rollouts (12.2k and 7.0k tokens, 37 and 35 hedges) each botched the modulus constant in opposite directions - one applied the 1/n root twice and carried k=2^(1/6), the other took a square root and carried k=8 - then spent thousands of tokens on a self-inflicted contradiction before recovering. Prior rounds tried to fix this with symbolic exponent lectures (verify k^n=|c|, split the modulus step) and both lost heldout, so this revision instead keeps the raw |z-a|^n=|c||z-b|^n form and adds a cheap numeric audit at one collinear point, which is what actually let the derailed rollouts detect the wrong k, and it drops the redundant x+iy completion-of-the-square cross-check.

This round's 8 rollouts split 4/4 and every one of the 4 failures ended at the 16384-token cap, never on a wrong committed answer: two of them had already reached the correct union value and then kept re-deriving and restating it until truncation, while the other two abandoned the invariance argument to hunt for a tangent line or an origin-to-side distance that determines the rotation angle and never closed that search. The winners instead computed one wedge area in the aligned orientation and terminated promptly. This revision keeps the rotation-partition proof but adds a named ban on the tangent-line/point-to-line detour that consumed two failures and an explicit stop-after-the-first-area instruction to kill the restatement loop that consumed the other two.

My 8 public rollouts scored 5/8 and all three failures terminated normally with wrong counts, every one of them an aggregation error at the last step: one reported the per-polynomial root cap as the whole answer, one assumed each polynomial contributes exactly one index, and one used the interpolation count (degree plus one) for a single group and never summed over groups. Rounds 3-5 showed that adding jargon-heavy prohibition or reject rules to the incumbent collapses both train and heldout, so this revision instead reframes the hint around the portable extremal principle (upper bound plus matching construction) and states the summation over all N groups as an ordinary jointly required step rather than a list of forbidden endings.

Train fell to 3/8 with the incumbent, and all five failures split into two mechanisms: three ran out of length after botching the reduction (one produced irrational roots, another a quadratic with four-digit coefficients) and never noticed that the reduction was wrong, while one solved the quadratic correctly but then assigned the translated vertex a y-value from the carried displacement instead of from f, putting the point off the graph and yielding a wrong area. The revision therefore adds a cheap, portable validity test on the reduced equation - the known vertex's x must satisfy it, since the degenerate coincident configuration trivially meets every stated condition - which both catches a mis-derived equation immediately and turns the remaining quadratic into a linear read-off, and it makes evaluating f the only sanctioned way to get a new vertex's y.

All 8 of my public rollouts scored 0 again: four asserted the delivery order is deterministically reversed (answering 1 and 0), two assumed uniformity over permutations plus 'each item equally likely to be last' (1/24 and 1/4), one mixed a correct-style branch product for part a with the same uniformity error for part b, and one exhausted its token budget on unstructured enumeration. Four also inverted the pile orientation, equating the bottom of the destination with the last item delivered rather than the first. Rounds 1-5 showed every long rewrite of the 83-token incumbent cost held-out, so this is a minimal edit that keeps the incumbent's wording and inserts only the two clauses the failures demand: a cheap two-sequence variability probe that kills both the forced-outcome and the equally-likely claims, and a position-to-arrival-index conversion before testing the event.

All 8 rollouts scored 0 (7 hit the 16384-token cap) with the identical root cause seen in rounds 1-5: each read the incumbent's 'linear functional' framing but still built a polynomial whose coefficients are the unknowns and whose argument is the condition number, producing a degree-2005 polynomial with only 2004 roots, then burned the budget resolving that phantom free factor and reported 1/2005, 0, or a harmonic sum; two also declared the system inconsistent from a mis-shaped toy. Since five prior rewordings of the abstract warning all lost heldout accuracy, this revision leads with a concrete row/column tabulation step that makes the swap impossible to commit, states the isolation move as a row combination with an explicit allowed-exponent constraint, and turns 'missing root or inconsistent' into a self-check trigger to rebuild rather than a rabbit hole.

6/8 public rollouts were correct; both failures shared one mode and it was not arithmetic - they equated the stated group count with the unit count, divided every listed total by it, saw each quotient come out whole, and treated that as confirmation, so the gcd/maximum-count step was never run. The incumbent already says group wording only imposes a multiple constraint, but it gives no way to detect that a passing candidate is non-maximal, and round 5 showed that merely front-loading that warning costs heldout (0.2125 down to 0.1125). So I kept the incumbent's order and length and added a concrete portable maximality test: after dividing by the candidate N the per-unit shares must have no remaining common factor, and any shared factor k means kN is also admissible.

All 8 public rollouts were correct again (8/8, 4.1k-5.6k tokens, none truncated), so the training question stays saturated and every remaining point is transfer. The one uniform waste is post-solution second-guessing: each rollout reaches the centered solution by roughly its midpoint, verifies the identity, and then spends the rest re-litigating whether another center, sign, or family could work (7-14 'wait' restarts and 11-20 're-check' detours per rollout), which is exactly the behaviour that ran out of room in round 1. This revision keeps the proven trigger, centered ansatz, factored both-branch condition, and symmetric-data steps intact and adds only a portable closure rule stating that verification ends the search, which should convert wasted re-derivation into budget on harder unseen problems.

Only 2/8 correct and all six failures hit the 16384-token cap; every one of them collapsed the block swap into a single transposition, declared the composite a product of disjoint 2-cycles, and answered 2, or thrashed between mutually inconsistent per-size counts (one even reported 12 for one size) without ever verifying anything. The revision states that swapping length-L blocks is L parallel position swaps rather than one transposition, adds a cheap falsification test (apply the FULL operation twice and compare) that kills the order-2 story immediately, and replaces expensive repeated whole-state rewriting with tracking a single label orbit and taking the lcm of orbit lengths.
